one_liner: Meta's AOT-bytecode JavaScript engine for React Native; roughly halves app start-up versus JavaScriptCore by skipping parsing at launch.
what_it_does: Hermes is a C++ JavaScript engine built for React Native start-up, size and memory: JavaScript is compiled ahead of time (hermesc / hermes -emit-binary) to a compact bytecode file that ships inside the app, and the VM (hvm or libhermes) runs that bytecode. It is the default React Native engine (Hermes since RN 0.70, the static_h-based Hermes V1 since RN 0.84, February 2026) and embeds through JSI, with hermes_abi, N-API and a hermes_sandbox directory also in API/. It is not a drop-in for V8 or JSC outside React Native: its embedding API differs and it omits some spec features (local eval, with, a runtime ES module loader).
how_it_is_fast: Start-up: parsing and compilation move to build time, so launch only loads precompiled, optimized register-based bytecode (variable-length instructions, 1-byte register operands, constants loaded through dedicated opcodes and a string table) instead of parsing source. Memory: Hades, a mostly concurrent snapshot-at-the-beginning mark-sweep old generation, plus pointer compression and small-integer encoding (HV32: 32-bit values with heap-boxed doubles that do not fit). Throughput in Hermes V1 (static_h) comes from a new compiler with type inference over untyped JS, an optional baseline JIT for hot functions, and optional AOT native compilation of typed JS.
when_to_use: React Native apps where cold-start time to first screen matters: Meta's Mattermost measurement shows 1.97 s to 0.96 s on a Galaxy S20 and 0.52 s to 0.19 s on an iPhone 12 Pro against stock RN on JavaScriptCore.
Memory-constrained mobile or embedded hosts running a large, known JS bundle that can be compiled to bytecode at build time (Android APK 13.9 MB smaller and 93 MB less memory in the same test).
UI threads that cannot tolerate long GC pauses: Hades reports 48 ms p99.9 pauses on 64-bit devices versus GenGC's 1.4 s p99 on Facebook for Android.
C++ hosts that want a JS engine much faster than QuickJS on Octane-style code (Hermes V1 interpreter about 1.6x-4.6x QuickJS per Meta's June 2025 chart) without bundling V8.
when_not_to_use: Peak-throughput server or desktop JS: no page read compares Hermes with V8 or with JavaScriptCore's full JIT on throughput, and Meta deliberately chose not to build a JIT for the legacy Hermes line (the static_h JIT is optional).

Code that depends on local eval, with, Symbol.species, spec-exact non-strict arguments behaviour, Function.prototype.toString source text or a built-in ES module loader: Hermes documents these as excluded or deviating.

Running untrusted JavaScript in-process: Hermes has had critical type-confusion CVEs exploitable by crafted JS (CVE-2020-1911, CVSS 9.8, fixed in hermes-engine 0.5.2), and Meta notes such bugs matter only if the app evaluates untrusted JS.
Apps that load JS source at run time rather than shipping bytecode: the start-up win comes from precompiled bytecode, so it does not carry over to source loaded at run time.
Small-footprint hosts that need a minimal, self-contained engine: the build needs CMake, Ninja, Python and ICU, and the iOS IPA grew 4.4 MB with Hermes in Meta's own test.

integration.form: shared lib (libhermes via JSI C++ API) plus CLI tools (hermes, hermesc, hvm, hbcdump); in React Native it is built and shipped by RN itself
integration.dependencies: CMake, Ninja, Python and ICU to build (libicu-dev on Linux); libreadline optional for the REPL
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; clang, gcc or Visual C++ (Visual Studio 2019 generator in the Windows instructions; CI now uses VS 2026)
integration.platforms: Android and iOS (primary), macOS, Linux, Windows; HV32 by default on Android and HV64 on iOS in Hermes V1; JIT availability per platform not documented in the sources read
integration.thread_safety: not documented in the sources read; Hades does its old-generation marking on a background thread on 64-bit devices (incremental, single-threaded on 32-bit)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: a supported engine swap inside React Native (the default since RN 0.70; RN 0.84 documents an opt-out back to legacy Hermes); outside React Native it exposes JSI, hermes_abi and N-API rather than V8's or JSC's embedding APIs, and its spec deviations can break code that runs on V8

gotchas: The headline numbers are first-party (Meta's React Native blog, 2022) on one app, Mattermost, timed from icon press to first screen with no published harness, run count, variance, engine versions or build flags; '51% faster' and '63% faster' are time reductions, about 2.05x and 2.7x as speed ratios (derived from page data). The baseline is JavaScriptCore in stock React Native, not V8.

The QuickJS-relative throughput charts (doc/blog 2025-07-15, Hermes V2 measured as hv32 with and without JIT) give no QuickJS version, compiler flags or hardware, and the repo's benchmarks/bench-runner only has Hermes, V8 and V8 --jitless runners (Hermes runs bytecode precompiled with -O), so the QuickJS columns cannot be reproduced from the repo; legacy Hermes is about level with QuickJS on zlib.

Bytecode is version-locked: Hermes bumped the bytecode version 98 to 99 for release 260318099.0.0 and prebuilt bytecode must be rebuilt; the README warns each Hermes release targets a specific React Native version and a mismatch can crash the app.

Hades trades throughput for pause time (more expensive write barriers, freelist allocation instead of bump-pointer, more fragmentation), and Promise is a bytecode polyfill whose microtask timing differs from the spec in some async and subclass cases.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Hermes over QuickJS, PrimJS or Escargot when you ship a React Native or other mobile app whose JS bundle can be compiled to bytecode at build time and start-up, memory and GC pauses matter most; pick QuickJS (or PrimJS) when you need a tiny, spec-complete engine with eval and ES modules from source text, and V8 when peak JIT throughput matters more than footprint.
verified_claims_summary: Meta measured the Mattermost React Native app with Hermes versus stock React Native on JavaScriptCore: start-up (icon press to first rendered screen) 0.96 s versus 1.97 s on a Samsung Galaxy S20 and 0.19 s versus 0.52 s on an iPhone 12 Pro, with memory 305 MB versus 398 MB and 107 MB versus 120 MB, the APK 13.9 MB smaller and the IPA 4.4 MB larger; engine versions, build flags and repetition counts are not published. Separate first-party bar charts (no hardware or QuickJS version stated) put the Hermes V1 interpreter at about 1.6x-4.6x and Hermes V1 with JIT at about 2.0x-5.6x QuickJS on Octane plus three React benchmarks.
status_note: Actively developed by Meta (default branch static_h, last commit 2026-10-05, Hermes V1 the React Native default since RN 0.84), MIT-licensed and buildable standalone with CMake, but its release cadence, bytecode versions and API are tied to React Native.
